title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
author: Dan Goodin
text:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

One connection, works every time, needs no retries

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

title: NASA unveils mysterious X-70 experimental aircraft using AI-generated image
author: Jeremy Hsu
text:
NASA has announced a new experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, that will supposedly feature reconfigurable flight-control technology and a modular design for swapping in different payloads. But much remains unknown about the aircraft’s design and development timeline, even as NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the X-plane could take flight within two years.

The mystery surrounding NASA’s newest X-plane was exemplified by the agency’s press release, including an apparently AI-generated image of the X-70, showing a dark silhouette vaguely resembling a military fighter jet obscured by smoke. The news was announced by Isaacman during the UP.Summit held at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 4.

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” Isaacman said. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next.”

title: Outshining established players, mid-season promotions and Grand Tour victories – Taking a closer look at 10 stand-out neo-pros of 2026
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
The first year as a professional cyclist is often one of finding a footing in the intensely competitive pelotons, where the dream of being paid to race a bike can become a brutal reality. There are some, however, that do just more than learn and survive in that first year – they step up to the challenge and thrive.

Some neo-pros entered the 2026 season with the weight of expectation already on their shoulders, such as Jarno Widar and Jakob Omrzel after steadily laying foundations and building blocks via years of racing in Europe through the junior and U23 ranks, accumulating results that put them in the spotlight along the way.

Others took a more unconventional path, such as Sandrine Tas, Lennart Jasch and Lauren Dickson, starting out in another sport and then discovering a talent for cycling later on. Then there are those, like Jasch and Talia Appleton, who at the start of the season were actually not yet even neo-pros but made such a splash in the development teams that a mid-season promotion to the next tier came early.

From the surprise breakthroughs to the long watched new stars of the professional peloton, we take a look at the achievements and path of 10 riders who have made such a big mark in their first season as a professional that it seems likely you'll be hearing about them on an increasingly regular basis through coming seasons.

This German rider wasn't on anyone's radar as one of the neo-pro's to watch at the start of this year for one simple reason, at that point he was still listed on the Tudor Pro Cycling development team roster.

Lennart Jasch came to cycling late, coming from speedskating, but has been quick to make a big impression since he signed up with a regional cycling team in 2024. After a year with the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe Rookies in 2025, Jasch made his potential crystal clear at the 2.Pro ranked Tour of the Alps when, having stepped up to take on an event with the senior team, he claimed victory on stage 4 from among a field packed with WorldTour riders. Not surprisingly after that he was quickly bumped up to that squad for the rest of the season. That, however, is not where his winning run ended with a stage win at Il Giro d'Abruzzo to prove his early season efforts were no fluke.

That left him heading into his final stage race of the season with what he said was 'absolutely no pressure' but undoubtedly a big opportunity . The newcomer to the world of cycling who had only just stepped up into the ProTeam level was being given a chance to take on a general classification tilt as team leader at Le Tour de Langkawi with the pre-race objective outlined as his team being a top five overall. He well and truly overshot that goal.

After the very first climbing challenge to Gunung Jerai on stage 2, Jasch was already in the overall lead with a 20 second margin, though other teams had multiple options lining up behind. There were no shortage of attempts to find ways to wear down the leader, but even as the temperature of the competition and environment continued to rise, Jasch kept a cool head. He displayed the patience and composure that many far more experienced players often find it hard to muster. Plus, while he was prepared to rely on his team, Jasch was also ready to take responsibility for jumping on a dangerous move and could also finish off the team effort in a way that meant he could not only hold onto, but also add to, his leading margin. It was a race that Jasch said would provide a 'first answer' as to how he may fare as a GC rider and that first answer is one that is bound to make his rivals sit up and take notice.

Sticking to the theme of skaters turned cyclists, let's take a look at Sandrine Tas. The 31-year-old this year turned a childhood passion and one time training tool into a profession this year. Tas switched from the ice to the road with her debut at this year's La Flèche Wallonne just months after competing in the speedskating at the Winter Olympics.

She had already made her cycling capabilities clear, coming eighth in the elite women's road race at the Belgian National Championships in 2025 and also winning two national level races. However, the first real test was launching into the professional peloton in the tough and talent packed one-day Women's WorldTour race, and Tas came through it with flying colours. She finished 57th, 3:35 off the winning time of Demi Vollering in a showing that clearly demonstrated an ability to manage the chaos of a top-tier peloton.

What's more, on just her sixth race day in the professional peloton the first win came on stage 1 of the Bretagne Ladies Tour. Then she followed it up with another on stage 3 which landed her in second overall at the three day 2.1 tour. A win, let alone two in a first season as a professional, is an impressive beginning, though more podium appearances and a Tour de France Femmes start were yet to come. In fact Tas even managed another top step before the season was over, with victory ahead of Charlotte Kool on stage 1 of the Eneco Tour to round out one extremely successful first year.

Australian rider Luke Tuckwell certainly wasn't heading into his first year as a professional without eyes on him, his second place overall at the Giro d'Italia Next Gen and top 10 at Tour de l'Avenir in 2025 made sure of that. He started the year at home at the Santos Tour Down Under , where he came fourth in the youth classification, and then as the season built so did the results.

At the Tour de Romandie, Tuckwell delivered his first WorldTour overall top 10, taking sixth among a strong field led by none other than Tadej Pogačar. That was impressive by itself, but it also opened up another opportunity, as it led to the decision to send the Australian to the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. That's when an already great season as a first year professional turned into a phenomenal one.

After a solid start to the race, stage 6 delivered an opportunity that Tuckwell wasn't going to let slip through his fingers. A huge break got away, with Tuckwell part of it, and while he helped his teammate Maxim Van Gils claim the stage win the Australian also finished third with a margin that comfortably shifted the rider up from twelfth overall to the very top spot.

It was a step up from the UAE Development Team for Federica Venturelli in 2026 straight into the world's top team, and while track was still a focus – which delivered plenty of success – there was no hiding in the peloton on the road. The Italian's very first race of the season was the 1.Pro Clásica de Almeria in late February and she went straight to the top step of the podium with a winning sprint from a reduced group of six.

There was then another victory at Dwars door de Westhoek in June, quickly followed by a second place in the opening stage of the Tour Féminin International des Pyrénées. At the end of three stages of racing she also walked away with the points classification. It's an impressive tally from just 16 days of racing as a professional and bodes well for what's to come when the all-rounder adds some more in 2027, particularly if the 2025 U23 European time trial champion manages to add some more races against the clock into the mix.

It was Jakob Omrzel who beat Luke Tuckwell to the top spot at the Giro d'Italia Next Gen in 2025 and the 20-year-old also delivered strong GC results as he stepped into the a new tier. That began with sixth overall at the Tour of the Alps in April, a top 10 at the Tour de Hongrie, third at Tour of Slovenia.

Then in the second half of the season it was time for the rider from Slovenia to take on his first Grand Tour, as the youngest rider at the Vuelta a España,and he did way more than just survive it. First there was a fourth place on the challenging uphill finish of stage 7. Then on stage 12 Omrzel got into a 30-man breakaway and then also rode away from it to cross the line solo and claim his first WorldTour win , and at a Grand Tour no less. In doing so he became the youngest Slovenian to win a Grand Tour stage, no small feat given this his compatriots in the peloton include Tadej Pogačar and Primož Roglič. Also in that moment he became the second youngest ever stage winner at the Vuelta, after Celestino Prieto who took his win in 1981.

The rider who is signed with Bahrain Victorious through till the end of 2029 also walked away from the Spanish tour with second in the youth classification and seventh overall. Though, perhaps, more importantly he left his first Grand Tour having gathered experience and tested his limits, which look set to stretch to considerable heights through the years ahead.

For Liv AlUla Jayco, there is plenty of pride wrapped up in the Australian summer, as it is the one time of the year when the nation's only Women's WorldTour Team gets to perform at home. There, too, is plenty of effort put into making the team is also taking the green and gold stripes of the national champions jersey back to Europe. Ruby Roseman-Gannon may have been the favourite from the squad to do just that, but Mackenzie Coupland, who had just stepped up from the Liv AlUla Jayco development squad at the start of the year turned out to be the one to claim the jersey after making a late move that stuck.

That meant a neo-pro year in the distinctive national champions kit for the first year professional, a big enough achievement on its own delivered in one of her very first races with the Women's WorldTour team. She was also the squad's top finisher at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race later that month, narrowly missing the podium with fourth and then in March, joined the development squad for a race and claimed a stage and the overall victory at Vuelta a Extremadura Femenina. A third place at La Périgord Ladies when then followed up with a spot on the Tour de France Femmes squad and a strong fourth at Chrono Féminin de Gatineau to help round out a first year in the professional peloton for the 21 year old.

After starting with such a strong opening round in Australia in 2026, there is no doubt there will be plenty of eyes on her to see what she can deliver in round two in 2027.

There was no shortage of focus on Jarno Widar in 2026 as he stepped up to the Lotto Intermarché WorldTour team from the development squad, having won the Kristallen Fiets young talent of the year award for a second year running plus delivered results that included victory at Liège–Bastogne–Liège U23, stage wins in the Giro NextGen and the Tour de l’Avenir as well as the European U23 road race title. It was a results list that meant he was ushered into the team with considerable fanfare, with the expectation that he would be doing far more than learning the ropes but would be supported to chase key results, in fact the 20-year-old even entered his first Grand Tour, the Vuelta a España, as team leader.

The first half of the season had its challenges, with illness and lingering knee injury keeping him away from racing for 16 weeks, though he made a solid mark soon after his return with fourth on the final stage of Tour de Suisse. He then upped the ante in his Vuelta debut, coming second on stage 4 behind Tadej Pogačar . There was also a fourth on stage 13 of the Spanish Grand Tour.

It was, however, the closing month of 2026 when Widar stepped up to deliver on the promise and to the top step, with a win Tre Valli Varesine and then his first WorldTour stage victory in the final day of racing at the Tour of Guangxi, which also clinched him the overall win. Those strong closing weeks are bound to help make the challenges of the early season feel like a distant memory and set the rider up as a focal point for the team in 2027, a year where the squad will be losing its former great hope, Arnaud De Lie.…

title: Why the Factor ONE Proves Specialized Needs a New Venge
author: Josh Ross
text:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I recently posted an article comparing the Specialized Tarmac SL9 and the Factor ONE . They are two of the most important road bikes of the last year (give or take) and the perfect foil for one another. Both are built to go fast, but they represent completely different philosophies of modern speed. Because I’ve had the opportunity to spend a lot of time on both, I wanted to answer the questions everyone is asking. This is all very straightforward stuff.

After I posted that story, I started reading the comments. I generally do my best to read everything across all the platforms where we post. But what I saw in the comments on this comparison was something I didn’t expect.

A lot of people think the Factor ONE is ugly. That’s expected. It looks nothing like most bikes and it is pushing about as far from the traditional silhouette as you can get for a road bike. When a design is that radical, it’s naturally going to turn some people off.

The simple explanation is that Factor wrapped the tube shapes around aerodynamic data and didn’t care much if the result looked weird. I could tell you that and move on, but I don’t think that’s the whole story. To see the reality, you have to look a little deeper at the feedback.

People calling it ugly was a given. What wasn’t expected is that most of those same critics openly acknowledged that the Factor ONE is the faster bike. You’d see things like, “The Factor might be faster, but it’s ugly,” or, “The Tarmac isn’t an aero road bike, it’s an all-rounder.”

Think about what that means for a second.

The Specialized Tarmac SL9 is one of the fastest road bikes to ever exist. Tour magazine tested it at 205 watts of drag in the wind tunnel at 45 km/h. That is exceptionally fast, but it actually sits outside of the top 12 bikes Tour has ever tested. The Factor ONE is indeed faster with a baseline score of 202 watts, and by optimizing it with different wheels, aero tires, and a 1x configuration, Tour was able to push that number down to 196.8 watts.

Objectively, that is a win. But you also have to think about how aerodynamic drag works. Tour tests at 45 km/h (about 28 mph) because that’s the practical floor for testing. If you go any slower, you start getting into the margin of error for the wind tunnel and the results get muddy. But what about you and me? Over 100 to 300-mile distances, my average speed tends to sit at a weirdly specific 16.7 mph. On a normal day, I actually cruise closer to 20 mph. If I am pushing hard on a shorter ride, anything sustained past a few minutes might see me hold a best of 24 mph.

At those real-world speeds, the physics change dramatically. Looking at the absolute best-case scenario for the Factor (the fully optimized 1x setup, similar to how I run my size 54 with a SRAM XPLR drivetrain and Zipp 454/858 NSW wheels). At 24 mph, we are looking at roughly a 5-watt advantage over the Tarmac. That is still something to be impressed with, although remember it did take some work after it came from Factor. Drop to a 20 mph cruise, and that gap shrinks to just 3 watts. Drop it to my long-distance average of 16.7 mph, and the aerodynamic advantage essentially disappears completely.

So, there is virtually zero watt savings at 16.7 mph, but there is a very real penalty on the scale. When I weighed both bikes ready-to-ride minus pedals, the Tarmac was a full kilogram lighter. That’s 6.5kg for the Tarmac versus 7.57kg for the ONE. Is the ONE actually faster?

None of this is an indictment of the very real speed Factor has wrestled from the ONE. I believe in stacking aerodynamic efficiency and finding watts wherever I can. In fact, if I had to choose between the two bikes, I’d pick the ONE (and I said as much in the comparison article). I understand that across a long ride, we spend the vast majority of our time at lower gradients, meaning aerodynamic benefits lead to a faster overall ride. We also harvest larger gains when we push the pace, even if those advantages shrink when we slow down.

The point is simply that Specialized is technically correct in the philosophy they are using as a guiding principle. The Tarmac isn’t the absolute fastest in the wind tunnel, but Specialized rightly points out that trading a few watts to save a full kilogram is a highly valid equation. The brand is also looking at racing holistically: when you are drafting in a pack, you lose many of the aerodynamic advantages that come from an aggressive frame profile anyway.

Another way to look at this is strictly as a consumer and not a WorldTour racer. I ride alone a lot, which is why I love focusing on aero performance. But if you ride in a group, it’s incredibly common to just cruise and chat on the flats, only to turn the hills into a race. In that real-world scenario, you legitimately might want to optimize for climbing, because that’s the only time you are actually competing. Or, you might just prefer the snappy feel of a light bike.

Which is all to say: the idea that the Factor is definitively faster isn’t really true. It is faster in some scenarios and slower in others.

What’s important, though, is that people believe it’s faster. The shape of the bike is the marketing. When you look at the Factor ONE and think, “That’s ugly, but it must be fast,” that visual leap is all that matters. Perception is reality, and the perception is that Factor owns speed.

And this is where Specialized is losing. The brand is the only one in the industry that owns its own wind tunnel, yet somehow consumers look at the modern lineup and assume the innovation has stalled. Perception sells bikes, and that is a long-term problem.…

title: 'I felt the bone snap' - Hannah Otto survives 40% gradients, snowy summit and fracture to set epic one-day Kilimanjaro summit record
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Hannah Otto (Scott Sports) added another endurance record to her resume on Wednesday, this one to an elevation of 19,300 feet above sea level. On November 4, she completed a Fastest Known Time (FKT) with Beyond the Summit: Kilimanjaro for World Bike Relief, becoming the first woman to use a mountain bike to summit Mount Kilimanjaro and descend in one day.

Her effort on the highest mountain in Africa almost came to an abrupt end with two miles to go, when she slipped in some mud and broke her tibia. She was able to remount her bike and pedal with one leg to complete the journey, a film crew nearby capturing the effort for a future film, though she refused assistance so the record would count, recorded as 'one day' for the FKT since it was a mark.

"Kilimanjaro FKT!! Mission accomplished! Dream come true! The first known woman to climb and descend Kilimanjaro in one day by bicycle," she posted to Instagram one day ago.

"From the dark hours of the early morning and listening to the monkeys scream at me in the rainforest to steep pitches over 40% gradients, to scrambling over rocks with a bike on my back, to a 19,300-foot [5895 metre] summit covered in snow this was the best experience of my entire life and also the hardest thing I’ve ever done.

"As if it wasn’t hard enough, with two miles to go I had a small crash. It was simple, just sliding out in some mud. But my foot got caught and I felt the bone snap. I laid in the mud feeling my dreams slip away, and that felt more painful than any broken bone. I crawled to my bike, used it as a crutch, and finished the final two miles pedaling with one leg to the finish.

"X-rays show a broken tibia. I think this shows that a dream may just be the most powerful thing in the world."

After an assessment at hospital in Tanzania, Otto told that she travel back to the US immediately for medical attention to repair a proximal tibia fracture.

"I was advised to fly home for further care and examination. I’m heading home from Africa today [Friday]. I have a consult with a surgeon on Tuesday and I’ll have more information then."

The Utah-based mountain bike specialist completed her fifth season as part of the Life Time Grand Prix two weeks before making the trip to Africa. She ended her run of four consecutive seasons in the top 10, missing the mark by just three points for 11th overall. Her best race finishes in the series this year were third at Little Sugar MTB and eighth at Leadville Trail 100 MTB, a race she won in 2022.

Otto has accumulated an eye-popping collection of FKTs, which she also uses as training for her endurance off-road racing. Last fall she set a new FKT for women on Mauna Kea , riding the 55-mile (88.5km) mountain road with 13,700 feet (4,175 metres) of climbing in Hawaii in 5 hours, 43 minutes and 50 seconds. She also has a trio of FKT records in high terrain US desert routes - Kokopelli Train, White Rim and Whole Enchilada.

While only 26.5 miles in distance (42.6km) in Tanzania, the main obstacle was elevation gain across the dormant volcano. The summit is just above 19,300 feet (5,895 metres) with five climate zones crossed from top to bottom.

Several days prior to her solo FKT, Otto made an initial ascent with a group and local crew, including a lead guide who had summited Kilimanjaro over 180 times. The 'first' summit was made on November 1.

"The entire crew made it to the top to celebrate this momentous moment together. Now we descend all the way back to the bottom and I’ll attempt to summit in just one day on November 3rd," she wrote on her social diary.

"After seeing this whole mountain piece by piece, it scares me. Things can change in an instant and the only constant is inconsistency. But that’s the entire point. I’m diving into the fear, I’m believing despite not knowing. I hope what anyone takes away from this attempt is the bravery to try without promise. We’re almost at $60K raised for World Bicycle Relief via The Intrepid Foundation!"

She said she realised her power on the bike would drop at the higher altitude, so she was keeping a close watch on her heart rate. "Instead of tracking miles I'm tracking elevation climbed."

Clad in a heavy coat, lined gloves and her helmet, Otto smiled for a photo when she was able to dismount and sit on the rock wall at the top of the mountain with a bright blue sky shining above.

"This film will be absolutely epic; that I’m sure of," Otto posted. The date of the film release is yet to be announced.

title: Redshift Releases Look and Shimano Compatible Mousetrap Pedal Adapters. Right Now They’re 25% Off.
author: Will Tracy
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Redshift Mousetrap pedal adapters (Photo: Redshift)

I’ll just say this up front: you don’t explicitly need Redshift’s Mousetrap pedal adapters. But then again do you really need most things out there? When I first saw these adapters that turn your clipless pedals into flat pedals, I wasn’t a hater, but I wasn’t convinced of their necessity, or who they are for. Who they are for, as it turns out, is me.

I keep SPD pedals on my around-town bike because it lets me go out and shred a little harder on any trip whether I’m grabbing groceries, visiting a friend, or just catching the sunset after work. But I don’t always want to put on riding shoes.

Can I get away with just riding with regular shoes on SPD pedals? Certainly, and I did it for years. Is life better now that I have these simple flat-pedal converters to toss on in seconds when I want them? Also certainly yes. The pedal platform for these is wide, grippy, and level—more than I can say for riding SPDs with regular shoes.

I’m not going to try to convince you that everyone needs these—you either have a use for them in your life or you don’t. You can pedal a bike with clipless pedals and regular shoes for quick trips around town no issue. But if you find yourself doing that regularly, the Mousetrap converters are a nice thing to have. It also means you can convert pedals in seconds, rather than maybe a couple minutes to swap in flat pedals. When you lay it out like that, it’s not a lot of time, but it is enough of a hassle that most of us, myself included, wouldn’t do it.

Now, Redshift is releasing the adapters for Look and Shimano SPD-SL road pedal styles. It’s essentially the same product, just modified to fit different pedal styles. Like with the SPD version, these adapters use the clip-in mechanism of your pedal to sit flush with the top of the pedal, provide an 80x105mm textured platform for grip, and clip on and off in seconds. When you’re not using them, a built-in magnet keeps them together so you don’t lose one between rides. There’s only a slight variation in weight between the versions due to their different clip-in mechanisms.

I just got a set of the SPD-SL version as well which I plan to keep in my car for when I drive to a ride with my road bike. Again, it’s not solving a huge problem in my life, but I’ll be plenty happy to have them for riding to lunch after the main ride.

Right now, Redshift is offering all three versions of the Mousetrap—SPD, SPD-SL, and Look—for 25% off as part of its early Black Friday Sale. Normally $59.99 USD, they are $44.99 right now.

Redshift says Crankbrothers Egg Beater pedals are next in the pipeline. Those pedals are definitely harder to ride with regular shoes, so I see even more of a use-case here for people who like the four-sided design.

title: Antonelli says 2027 preparation starts now
text:
New world champion Kimi Antonelli says he is treating the final races of the season as the beginnings of his campaign to retain the title next year.

The Mercedes driver became the youngest champion in Formula 1 history, in only his second season, when he clinched the title in Mexico City last weekend.

Antonelli, 20, has his first race since tying up the title at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix this weekend.

"I'm actually very excited to be here," he said. "It's a good opportunity for me to, first of all, you know, try to finish the season on a top, but I also feel like that my 2027 preparation starts now.

"It's going to be important to finish the season well, strong, in order to have the confidence and also to be able to get the confidence ahead of 2027."

Antonelli visited the property of the family of the late Ayrton Senna on Tuesday and sat in one of the legendary three-time champion's Lotus cars from the 1980s.

He is wearing a new helmet design paying tribute to Senna at Interlagos this weekend.

Antonelli reflected on his achievement on media day at the track on Thursday.

"I would have liked a bit more time to just even digest what happened," he said. "I had such a crazy sequence of events in these days. I won the championship, then spent time with the Senna family, which was already an incredible event. So definitely, I would have liked a bit more time to just sit down and like reflect and realise what happened."

He said the idea of being world champion "still feels surreal".

One of his most treasured moments on Sunday in Mexico was when Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen hoisted him on to their shoulders on the podium after the race.

Antonelli said: "I already framed the picture and definitely will put it on the wall because it's such a moment. Who would have said it? I wouldn't have expected to celebrate my title in that way. So definitely when they picked me up was the cherry on top of the cake.

"I will always be thankful towards them for doing that because, first of all, to receive that from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is very special.

"And also even more special because it was real. It was something that they actually wanted to do.

"So it was a very special moment and definitely I hope I can see them again to thank them properly with a bit of calm because it was just very special."

title: Superprestige Middelkerke: Joran Wysure steals the win as Michael Vanthourenhout has heated run-in with Cameron Mason
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
Joran Wysure (Corendon-Crelan) claimed the victory in the nighttime Superprestige Middelkerke , overcoming a series of mishaps to take the high-speed race ahead of series leader Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw). Kevin Kuhn (Heizomat Cube) finished a close third.

The race wasn't without drama, as Cameron Mason (777tv) had a late run-in with Vanthourenhout and endured an earful from the Belgian after the race.

On lap eight of 10, Vanthourenhout tried to keep Mason from passing in a turn before the sand pit, bumping Mason in the shoulder. But he paid for his aggression, losing his balance in the off-camber and losing a few positions. The incident hardly affected the results.

The nighttime Superprestige Middelkerke started with a full field under the lights with Maes Hendrikx (Bomba Join) getting the quickest start when the lights turned green, but he was tailed closely by Vanthourenhout heading into the first corner.

Now the series leader, Vanthourenhout is a top contender for the European championships and was keen to get a top result, but held back in the early laps to save his energy for Sunday.

A crash disrupted the back of the field but at the front, it was Vanthourenhout's teammate Gerben Kuypers who took charge of setting the pace in the first laps. The pace and the numerous short, sharp climbs and technical turns steadily whittled down the number of riders in the leading group, even though there were no major attacks.

Mason took the lead heading into the fifth lap, and his pace made Kuypers suffer. Vanthourenhout took to the front on lap six to let his teammate rejoin, but a surge from Wysure broke things up again but a mistake in the barriers knocked him out of the lead group.

On lap eight, Wysure was still pushing the pace when Vanthourenhout ran into Mason and lost touch with the leading group briefly. Then, it was Mason's turn to tumble on the barriers, but he was quickly back up and riding, and on Vanthourenhout's wheel.

Wysure led at the start of the penultimate lap, with Kuhn, and Jente Michels (Alpecin-Premier Tech) in pursuit. Vanthourenhout found Kuypers again and latched onto Michels' wheel with Mason just behind.

The evening dew caused mayhem again as Wysure slid out in a greasy turn and his spill allowed Kuhn to join him, and it wasn't long before the rest of the chasers were in contact. Kuhn surged into the lead, gaining a second over Wysure who was rattled by the barriers. Kuhn crossed the line at the bell with Wysure and Vanthourenhout on his wheel.

The Corendon-Crelan rider managed to get to the lead, wanting the freedom to pick his own lines and set the pace. He used the downhill sections to gain a few seconds, but Vanthourenhout was on the hunt. Wysure overcame his mental block and cleared the barriers cleanly, he passed the greasy corner without slipping and went into the final stretch with enough of a lead to win the race without a challenge.

title: What Could Cervélo, Beats, Rapha, and Bose Tell Us About Cannondale’s Future?
author: Josh Ross
text:
Cannondale is packing up its Connecticut headquarters and leaving the state where it was founded 55 years ago. As parent company Pon.Bike consolidates North American operations into California, the brand is losing its historic home. What will this mean for a storied American brand?

Before I started writing for Velo , I spent over 20 years working for ad agencies as a creative director, making ads for some of the biggest brands in the world, including Samsung, Pepsi, IBM, and more. If you ever watched the TV show Mad Men, I was Peggy. Did I have a lot of martini lunches? That’s a story for another day.

​My job was to create ads that emotionally connected with consumers, protecting the most important asset these Fortune 500 companies had—their brand. So when I read the news about Pon.Bike closing Cannondale’s U.S. headquarters and consolidating operations within its portfolio, I paused.

Cannondale is closing its U.S. headquarters in Wilton, Connecticut. According to Bicycle Retailer, that means all 143 employees located there will be affected. Sales and operations are reportedly consolidating to Pon.Bike’s other American location in Santa Cruz, CA, where the holding company already has sales teams that handle the Cervélo and Santa Cruz Bicycles brands. Cannondale’s global HQ will relocate to Woudenberg, Netherlands. And R&D will remain in Freiburg, Germany, where it has operated for several years. According to reports, the first moves begin December 21, 2026, and will run in phases through the end of 2027.

​But a headquarters isn’t a brand. It’s a building. So nothing should really change, right? Maybe. For the Cannondale brand, I think it’s more than that.

The Cannondale story starts in 1971 in Wilton, Connecticut, where Joe Montgomery and Murdock MacGregor began making bike bags and trailers, pouring the proceeds into bike frames. They named those creations Cannondale, inspired by the nearby Metro-North train station.

​What came next was fifty years of bravado and innovation, building cycling curiosities that pushed the industry and grabbed people’s attention, for better or worse. From the Lefty fork (a single-sided suspension fork that soon became the stuff of legend) to the Hollowgram crankset (an ultra-light, super-stiff crank with an innovative two-piece bonded, hollow aluminum construction). Some ideas were more successful than others, but each carried that underdog spirit, the same scrappiness reminiscent of the organization’s early days.

​So what’s the secret sauce? Companies that create truly unique products do so by cultivating a culture of creativity. An environment where ideation and execution are celebrated, even if it is a little unorthodox. Originality is fueled by freedom. The space to dream up something different, weird, and unconventional. Sometimes that dream defines a category like the Synapse, blazing a trail for the endurance road bike category. Sometimes it’s a little less spectacular, like the familiar creak of the BB30 bottom bracket. Cannondale’s pioneering spirit had a home on the East Coast, and now, that space is being broken apart and shipped all across the world. Which begs the question…

To say exactly what the future holds for Cannondale is anyone’s guess. However, as a marketer, that’s where I turn to the next best thing…case studies. I looked at a variety of brands to see what happens when a company is ripped from its roots, when founders leave, and when they stick to their guns.

If you hark back to 2006, you’ll remember Beats by Dre, a Los Angeles headphone company started by the one and only Dr. Dre and longtime head of Interscope Records, Jimmy Iovine. While Beats sold headphones, they exported the energy of LA. The brand was steeped in West Coast hip-hop culture. The products looked amazing, sounded great, and consumers agreed, big time. Bloomberg Businessweek reported that at its peak in 2011, Beats held 64% of the U.S. premium headphone market. Then, in 2014, Apple acquired Beats for $3 billion. Dre and Iovine eventually left, and before long, the brand fizzled. LA energy gave way to Silicon Valley tech. Where’s the brand today? You can still buy Beats within the Apple ecosystem, but the revenue numbers are hard to pin down. In earnings calls, Apple doesn’t break out Beats revenue. Perhaps that’s all you need to know: a cultural giant reduced to a line item too small to report.

​Meanwhile, another headphone manufacturer is Bose. The company never sold. They never left their headquarters in Framingham, Massachusetts. And Dr. Amar Bose, founder and MIT professor, even gave the majority of the non-voting shares to the university where he taught for over 40 years. Why? He believed that a publicly held company could never innovate the same way that a private one could. So he gave the shares away. This is a story of commitment, principles, and, most importantly, what happens when founders stick to their vision, stay planted in their corporate roots, and weave their philosophy and vision into the brand’s fabric. While revenue numbers aren’t publicly reported, we can rely on the fact that Bose has outlasted every acquisition wave in the audio industry. Still independent, still in Framingham, and still the brand synonymous with great audio.

It would be impossible to do this article without talking about Rapha. What started in 2004 as Simon Mottram’s love letter to cycling culture, style, and functionality then exploded into a consumer obsession, with annual reports showing Rapha’s revenue growing 25–30% year over year, ending January 2017 at £63 million. According to The Guardian, Walmart’s Walton family stepped in and acquired the brand for a reported £200 million (approximately $254 million USD at the time). Mottram stepped down as CEO in 2021. And since the buyout, Rapha has not posted a single profitable year, reporting nine consecutive annual losses. Not to mention multiple CEOs and declining revenue.…

title: Deep-red Kansas votes for change as patience wears thin with Trump: ‘The economy is really taking a beating’
author: Gaya Gupta in Junction City, Kansas
text:
Bills have soared in rural state buffeted by tariffs and war in Iran – and Democrat Adam Hamilton’s stunning upset shows how deep economic frustrations run

L inda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and interested, in politics. Her father was a photographer who took portraits of political leaders in Washington, while her grandparents were farmers who cared deeply about their industry.

In 2024, Olson’s research led her to Donald Trump . She trusted that the then-former president would improve their economic realities in Junction City, Kansas – where she was born and raised – if he returned to the White House.

But two years later, life is just more expensive. Last winter, Olson was forced to spend $700 on medication while in between insurance plans, and skipped out on doses to stretch it out longer. Her grocery bills are unrecognizably high. And fuel prices are about a dollar per gallon more expensive than last year.

“I thought at the time that he was the better choice of what we had,” Olson said of Trump in 2024. Instead, he had been acting to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”.

With frustrations like these looming large across the state, Kansans this week elected a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in nearly a century. It was a stunning upset in what was, until recently, thought to be a reliably red stronghold.

“I’ve seen what Roger Marshall did over the eight years or so that he’s been doing this,” said Olson, of the defeated Republican senator. “And I thought, it’s time we get fresh blood up there.”

Hamilton won, in part, by flipping six counties that backed Trump in 2024 and Marshall in 2020 – a sign that, even in more remote, and traditionally conservative, areas, patience with Trump and the Republican party is wearing thin.

“Not everybody that voted for Trump is part of this cult of personality that Trump has tried to make the Republican party into,” said Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, located in one of those six flipped counties.

“There are certainly people in Kansas that are like that: they’re pretty conservative, but they’re not beholden to Trump. And so I think one of the things this election did is peel off those people.”

M ost of Kansas is made up of farmland, encompassing nearly 45m acres and employing nearly one in five Kansans. Pastures, dotted with grazing cows and their calves, hug the state’s highways. Junction City is surrounded by its famed toffee-colored prairies, so expansive that untouched grassland stretches out to the horizon on both sides of the interstate.

Kansans who ranch and farm here, in the most rural corners of the state, remain deeply Republican, according to Smith. But neighboring communities such as Junction City and Emporia, where he teaches, depend heavily on the agricultural economy and have felt the impact of the strains on farmers.

“The people that live here aren’t actually farmers,” he said. “And they’re more likely to swing over to the other party because the economy is really taking a beating.”

David Aguirre, a 25-year-old who was born and raised in Junction City, and works at a Mexican restaurant, El Patron Dos, said that when the rest of the county is suffering, so does his work.

“It has, like, a domino effect for families,” he said. “If they’re not doing their best, they’re not gonna come out to eat, and then that affects staff, and cooks, and so on.”

While grocery shopping on Wednesday afternoon, Janet Grimm, who considers herself an independent, lamented her rising bills. Everything she picked out from the aisles was tagged with a red and yellow “sale” sticker, a conscious choice she needs to make now.

Checking out with just a handful of items – eggs, chicken, some deli meat, two cucumbers and powdered sugar for the banana bread she was planning on making later that day – her total rang up to over $60.

Grimm voted for Hamilton, and felt hopefully that he would be able to improve the economy for people like her. “I really have faith that they’re going to do good,” she said.

H amilton – whose campaign slogan was “leading from the middle” – followed an increasingly reliable playbook in Kansas, Smith suggested, in which candidates position themselves as moderate and distant from the national Democratic party. In his victory speech on Tuesday, Hamilton emphasized to a packed room of supporters that he would seek greater collaboration between parties during his tenure, to “solve problems like it used to be”.

“I’m going to tell you a little secret. I want to become Jerry Moran’s best friend,” said Hamilton, referring to the state’s other senator – a Republican.

“For the rest of the United States, in deeply red Kansas, the heart of America, I want us to model what it looks like when thoughtful people actually work together to solve problems, instead of slinging mud at each other.”

Channeling his years as the pastor of a megachurch, Hamilton recounted the story of the Good Samaritan – in which a Samaritan stopped to help a man who was beaten on his way from Jerusalem to Jericho – as a way to illustrate the importance of Democrats and Republicans helping out one another.

“If Jesus were telling this parable to a room filled with Democrats , he’d say, ‘And there was a Republican who came along and stopped and helped the man,’” said Hamilton. “If he was talking to a room filled with Republicans, he’d say, ‘And there was a Democrat who came along and stopped.’”

Every county in Kansas shifted to vote more Democrat in this year’s Senate race. Still, many areas of the state remain staunchly Republican, and no moderate candidate is likely to change that, said Smith.

“It’s still a pretty conservative state,” he said. “Let’s not get too hasty here.”…

title: Russell to have 'deep, deep look in mirror'
text:
George Russell says he plans to have a "deep, deep look in the mirror" to work out how he can improve after a disappointing 2026 season.

The Mercedes driver has watched team-mate Kimi Antonelli dominate on his way to becoming the youngest Formula 1 champion in history, while Russell has won only three races compared with the Italian's nine, despite starting the year as championship favourite.

Russell says luck has not been on his side, but wants to ensure he does everything he can to understand why he has lacked pace.

The Briton said: "It wasn't meant to be this season but you also need to look at yourself in the mirror and think: 'What could I have done better'?

"Is all of the misfortune truly misfortune? Or is it actually things in our control that could have been better?

"So you need to just have a deep, deep look in the mirror and pick yourself up again and go from there."

Antonelli says 2027 preparation starts now

How to follow Sao Paulo Grand Prix on the BBC

Russell said he and his team had analysed the season so far and worked out that he has had a trouble-free run in only six of this season's 20 races.

"These issues constantly keep popping up but unfortunately this always seems like it's on my side of the garage," he said.

"We concluded we've only had six races from the 20 where we've had a clean weekend. So to think 14 of those weekends have had issues is unbelievable.

"We need to look to understand why that is, if there's something we are overlooking or if it's just pure misfortune. At the moment it does seem like it's more misfortune than anything.

"In a normal season you might have two weekends or three weekends where there are issues. We've had three quarters of this season and that has been incredibly unfortunate."

He said it was the fact that he had been struck by another technical glitch that made him skip his media duties after last weekend's Mexico City race, rather than the fact Antonelli had just won the title.

Russell, who started second to Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, had a loss of power on the run to the first corner when the electrical part of the power-unit did not reply properly.

He was swamped by the field, and then collided with Isack Hadjar's Red Bull at Turn Six, earning himself a 10-second penalty. He finished sixth and dropped from second to fourth in the drivers' championship, behind Antonelli, Max Verstappen and Hamilton.

"In racing you always pick yourself back up and for me the best way to pick myself back up was getting out of there," Russell said on media day for this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

"It was as simple as that, really. I was just very upset with missing out on the chance of a good result because the championship for me was already over but I just couldn't believe how things had panned out again.

"In that moment, yeah, I just wanted to get out of there.

"I think I'm 99% of the time a true professional and I try not to spit my dummy out, but sometimes missing out on doing the press – OK, it's not ideal but not the end of the world.

"Moments like that you don't really want to deal with it."

text:
Aniek van Alphen (777tv) pulled off her first victory of the season in the nighttime Superprestige in Middelkerke , soloing away from the field on the second lap and maintaining a strong advantage to the finish. The result signalled she will be a strong competitor at the upcoming European Championships in Zeddam on Saturday.

Defending European champion Inge van der Heijden (Crelan-Corendon) couldn't chip away at Van Alphen's lead after missing the attack as she was caught in traffic in the early laps. However, she held on for second place, conserving her energy after distancing Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen), who bobbled in the final lap and had to settle for third.

The nighttime round of the Superprestige had a small women's field with the European Championships just two days away. While the race was missing top rider Lucinda Brand, 27 women toed the line under the bright lights in Middelkerke.

After following closely as Hélène Clauzel (777tv) took the hole shot, Defending champion Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) remained at the head of the race for the first lap.

But on the next one, she bobbled on one of the many short, steep climbs and had to chase Van Alphen, who opened up a lead of six seconds at the start of lap three.

Fouquenet continued to fade as European champion Van der Heijden caught Clauzel and set off in pursuit of Van Alphen. Betsema latched on during the fourth lap to form a three-rider chase.

Clauzel began to struggle, losing touch with Van der Heijden and Betsema, and by the end of lap four, the European champion was 10 seconds behind, with Betsema just ahead of Clauzel at 15 seconds by the start of the fifth lap.

It was Van der Heijden and Betsema chasing together with two laps to go, with a 14-second deficit to Van Alphen, with Clauzel and Fouquenet further behind.

Betsema surged on lap six, bringing the gap to the leader down to ten seconds but Van Alphen matched her acceleration and extended her lead on the sinuous second half of the circuit and started the final lap with 16 seconds over the two chasers.

title: Israel’s Herzog yet to decide on who should form government as Eisenkot secures significant backing
author: Jason Burke International security correspondent and agencies
text:
President calls on all parties to help avoid new election after Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs fell short of majority

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, was due to meet Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, on Thursday with less than a week left before he decides which of the two men should first try to form a government.

A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority , dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.

In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.

Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80% , transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.

The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.

“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.

Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members , Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.

Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.

Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.

“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility ​rests upon us,” Herzog said.

Netanyahu remains prime minister ​in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another ‌election, which must be held if no candidate ‌succeeds.

Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on ​an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast ​doubt on the results, accusing Israeli Palestinian-led parties of stealing ​the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.

Israel’s Central Election Committee said ​on Wednesday that the election’s integrity ‌ had not been compromised . The ​head of the committee, the supreme court justice ​Noam Sohlberg, has called on the country’s elected officials to protect public trust.

“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. He said high voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing.

Netanyahu’s allies on the far right, including Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

title: Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother ‘person of interest’ in child sexual abuse inquiry
author: Caroline Davies
text:
Philippine official says there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but he’s not yet being treated as a suspect

The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.

The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.

He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.

More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.

He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.

Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.

Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”

He added: “We will know in the next few days.”

Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.

Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind ”.

Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.

Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.

Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.

title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
text:
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise interest rates on Thursday in what would be the first increase to the benchmark rate for more than three years.

Most analysts are predicting an rise from 3.75% to 4% in a move that would increase the cost of borrowing for individuals and businesses, but boost savers.

The Bank rate has fallen from its 2023-24 peak of 5.25%, although the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has left the rate unchanged at its last six meetings.

Rising inflation, driven primarily by the cost of petrol and diesel, will push policymakers into an interest rate hike, analysts suggest.

The announcement will be made by the Bank at 12:00 GMT on Thursday.

Close attention will also be paid to any hints from the MPC on the future direction of interest rates.

"The decision is increasingly less about whether rates reach 4% and more about what follows after that," said Chris Cheverall, head of UK at trading platform CMC Markets.

"A quarter-point rise is already widely expected, but the Bank now has to balance inflation that is still too high against an economy where the growth outlook has weakened sharply."

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation is well below its peak of a few years ago but has been heading back up and is expected to go higher.

It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target.

The ongoing impact of the Iran war, primarily on the cost of energy and fuel, has filtered through to the UK inflation rate. Millions of domestic energy customers are braced for a hefty rise in prices in January.

The Bank of England last raised rates in August 2023.

Its base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.

Were the Bank rate to rise, there would be an immediate impact on the 510,000 tracker mortgage-holders.

A 0.25 percentage point rise would mean a £31 increase in monthly repayments for someone with a typical tracker home loan, according to calculations by banking trade body UK Finance.

The 470,000 mortgage-holders on variable deals would need to wait for their lender's reaction to any Bank rate rise. Typically, a 0.25 percentage point rise would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments.

The picture for those on fixed deals is more nuanced.

While their monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are, and lenders have already "priced in" the expected rate rise when quoting new deals.

As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

It means anyone rolling off a five-year deal faces a much bigger mortgage bill.

Broker L&C said that average mortgage rates offered by the 10 biggest lenders suggested some borrowers now faced paying almost £5,000 more each year in repayments on a £200,000 mortgage over 25 years than those who secured a remortgage deal in 2021.

Five years ago, the average five-year fixed remortgage rate among the 10 biggest lenders was 1.30%.

Relatively high fixed rates have prompted some people to consider choosing trackers, in the hope that the rate would be lower, even if the Bank rate rises in the coming months.

"The right choice ultimately depends on borrowers being confident they can stomach future rises. The devil is in the detail," said Rachel Springall from Moneyfacts.

The cost of some other new loans could be influenced by the Bank rate.

Savers, on the flipside, could see the interest rates offered to them improve in light of any rise in the Bank rate.

Ultimately, lenders - as well as policymakers at the Bank of England - are having to judge what may happen to the UK's economic outlook which is highly connected to changes in international events.

title: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report
author: Owen Myers
text:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.

A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.

The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education.

The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of the popular groups BTS and Katseye ) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”.

In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe representatives said the company adheres to child-protection laws and works hard to make sure its artists work and train in safe conditions.

NewJeans are one of the decade’s most popular K-pop acts. In 2023, the five-member group followed Blackpink to become the second Korean girl-group to score a number one album on the Billboard charts. In November 2024, the band made global headlines when they announced their decision to leave the label amid contract disputes and claims that Ador had deliberately undermined their careers.

Band member Hanni alleged that NewJeans were mistreated by the label and accused Ador of “deliberate miscommunications and manipulation” in a statement to South Korea’s parliament last year.

Ador has consistently maintained that they did not violate their duty. “A unilateral claim that trust has been broken does not constitute valid grounds for termination of a contract,” the label said in a statement.

The label sued band member Danielle, a member of her family and the band’s producer in December 2025 for a total of nearly $30m for damages and a contract break penalty.

Hybe representatives told the New York Times that its exit penalty fees do not exceed industry standards.

In July, the group promised that 2026 would be the “summer of NewJeans”, with a teaser showing the group as a four-piece sans Danielle. New music has yet to emerge.

The new reports expose the shadowy world of K-pop contracts and shine a light on the restrictive conditions that the genre’s biggest stars can be subject to.

By the time they signed their contracts, the NewJeans members – Minji, Hanni, Haerin, Hyein and Danielle – had already clocked in years of training in K-pop “boot camps” which taught vocal training, choreography and foreign language education.

Schedules were strict, one source told the New York Times, and it was not unusual for rehearsals to stretch as late as 2am. NewJeans’s youngest member, Hyein, was 12 at the time.

After the band members received their exclusive contracts with Ador in January 2022, the parents of one member requested multiple changes. They were told that if they did not sign the contract in its current form, “the contract itself” could be reconsidered.

In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe said its contracts were legal and negotiated in good faith, with protections in place for the artist as well as the label’s investment in them.

That contract struck government language that forbade performers working for “excessive periods of time”. It also stipulated that the band would have to repay a significant percentage of the plastic surgery costs that are common in K-pop.

“We do not even recommend cosmetic surgery or procedures against an individual’s wishes,” Hybe said in a statement.

The NewJeans contract also granted Ador rights to use the band members’ “name, photographs, likeness, handwriting, voice and any other elements” in perpetuity, in a level of ownership that goes further than government recommendations for such rights to end at the point of contract termination.

The clause also grants Ador the right to use the NewJeans members as AI chatbots or clones.

The Guardian has reached out to Hybe for comment.

title: 'Purely from results, I'd say it definitely wasn't good'– Geraint Thomas admits challenging season for Netcompany Ineos
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
In a partial review of Netcompany Ineos' season, team Director of Racing Geraint Thomas conceded that 2026 "definitely wasn't good" from a results standpoint, although he did point out several positive aspects of the year.

Speaking with Decathlon CMA CGM Directeur Sportif Luke Rowe on the podcast, Thomas accepted that the team was a long way from where it once was when he, Chris Froome, and Bradley Wiggins were dominating Grand Tours. However, he pointed out several of the team's successes as they look to progress to their former dominant position.

"People have kind of said, 'oh, you know, you can say was our season good or bad?' And purely from results, I'd say it definitely wasn't good," Thomas said.

"I feel like Dorian [Godon], Oscar [Onley], and Kévin [Vauquelin] are all new to the team and that takes a bit of gelling. I think the fact that they executed is a big plus. I think they all learned then the next phase of that plan. And I think they'll all take that forward, and it's part of that growing."

The three new additions were among Netcompany Ineos ' highest performers in 2026. Godon was the team's top rider, winning seven times, including five stages across Paris-Nice, Volta a Catalunya, and Tour de Romandie.

Vauquelin, meanwhile, won the Giro d'Abruzzo and took fourth at Paris-Nice, and Onley took a stage win and second overall at the Vuelta a Burgos before taking sixth overall and best young rider at the Vuelta a España.

Thomas said the team was making progress, having "gone up the ladder a couple of steps" with their standout results.

"I think it's all learning and stuff as well, and even though results weren't particularly sensational, we had a lot of wins, but they were like smaller wins. It wasn't like any big wins, really," he said.

"It's all about that progression, and it's where you're starting from as well. This might be a headline now, but let's just say we're at 20% of what we used to be, to pick a number – you can't just go from 20 to 80 straight away.

"It's like climbing a ladder, isn't it? It's the same thing with a team, and I think we've gone up the ladder a couple of steps, for sure. We slipped a few times as well, but that's all part of it."

Other standout performances of Ineos' season included Filippo Ganna's Dwars door Vlaanderen triumph and Thymen Arensman 's ride to fourth place at the Giro d'Italia, his best-ever Grand Tour result.

"Great to see Pippo win Dwar Doors, the rest pretty flat, really. But it's kind of like that's what's always kind of been with our team as well, isn't it?" Thomas said, summing up the Classics season.

"[The Giro] was a bit more of a traditional sort of Grand Tour, wasn't it? Jonas was the outstanding favourite, but the way Visma rode was a bit more old school – controlling the harder days, and there was the race for the podium behind. Out of the three, it was a bit more kind of what you're used to.

"Thymen was 30, 40 seconds off the podium. I think it was a massive step forward if you just take him in isolation, from previous years. Just psychologically, a lot more consistent.

"He's done a lot of work with Steve Peters this year, and I think it definitely paid off, and the combination with his coach worked really well. It's the best Grand Tour result he's ever had. He was super consistent, there were no big standout mistakes, and I think that's a big positive for him."

The team was set for something of an overhaul for the 2027 season, with Ganna among the notable names on the outgoing list as several promising younger riders come on board.

Leading the list is the highly-rated junior world champion Benjamín Noval , who joins alongside fellow Spaniard Markel Beloki and former Tour de l'Avenir champion Joseph Blackmore. With 22 riders confirmed for 2027, there'll be more to come from Ineos in the transfer market before next season gets underway at the Tour Down Under.

'It's about time' - BMC enter women's peloton with Basque Laboral Kutxa team partnership
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Swiss bike brand BMC are set to make their first foray into the women’s peloton for many years, partnering with a Spanish ProTeam, Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi.

The deal, which is with the team’s Basque Country parent organisation Fundación Euskadi, will see the team not only riding their Teammachine SLR 01 frame sets, but also using their cockpits and wheels.

BMC have been a presence in the men’s peloton for some years, and currently provide bikes to the Tudor Pro Cycling Team. Before that, they worked with AG2R Citroën, Dimension Data, CCC and, obviously BMC Racing. However, they have not worked with a women’s team since at least the creation of the UCI Women’s WorldTour in 2016.

The company recently teased the partnership with a press release, saying "it’s about time we saw BMC bikes in both the men’s and Women’s Grand Tours," and the partnership has now been announced. As Laboral are one of the sport’s second-tier ProTeams, they have realised their desire to be present at the biggest women’s stage races.

"This partnership represents an exciting new chapter for BMC," said BMC’s head of marketing, David Heine. "As one of the brands that supported women's cycling early on, we are proud to return to the highest level of the sport with Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi.

"Women’s racing is thrilling, inspiring, dynamic, and growing rapidly worldwide. We look forward to supporting the team with our performance-driven bikes and proudly cheering for the riders throughout the season."

Laboral Kutxa have been riding at UCI level since 2020, starting life as Continental level team before moving up to ProTeam in 2025. During the 2026 season they rode Chinese XDS bikes and Shimano groupsets, it is not yet known whether Shimano will remain on board.

The president of Fundación Euskadi, Iñaki Isasi, is rightfully pleased with the partnership. "Their technical standards and culture of performance correspond to the ambitions of Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi. This support allows us to approach the season with confidence and continue to grow our women's team at the highest level."
